title: IRDAI's New Master Circular Cuts Insurer Share-Transfer Fee, Tightens IPO And Merger Disclosures
seo_title: IRDAI Cuts Insurer Share-Transfer Approval Fee
meta_description: IRDAI's 2 November 2026 master circular cuts the insurer share-transfer approval fee to Rs 10 lakh and sets fresh IPO and merger disclosure rules.
court: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI)
case_name: Master Circular on Registration, Capital Structure, Transfer of Shares and Amalgamation of Insurers, 2026
citation: IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/142/11/2026 dated 2 November 2026, issued under the IRDAI (Registration, Capital Structure, Transfer of Shares and Amalgamation of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, as amended by the 2026 Amendment Regulations notified 30 July 2026
body: An insurer looking to change hands, bring in a new investor, or merge with another company in India now works under a freshly consolidated rulebook from the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. The regulator's master circular of 2 November 2026, issued under its Registration, Capital Structure, Transfer of Shares and Amalgamation of Insurers framework, replaces the 2024 version of the same circular and folds in changes that followed amendments to the underlying regulations notified on 30 July 2026, after the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act, 2025.

The most concrete change is a fee cut. The circular records that the 2026 amendment regulations reduced the processing fee payable under the proviso to Regulation 22(4) for an application seeking approval to transfer shares in an insurer, from Rs 50 lakh to Rs 10 lakh. Fees already paid before the amendment took effect are not refundable, so the relief runs only to transactions filed afterward. For a promoter or strategic investor negotiating a stake sale in an Indian insurer, that is a direct cut in the cost of getting the regulator's sign-off, separate from any advisory or legal fees the deal itself carries.

That relief is paired with a new cost elsewhere. An application for a no-objection certificate for a new insurer's registration, filed on or after the amendment's notification date, must now carry a processing fee under Regulation 6(1)(ba), where earlier filings made before that date were exempt. Promoters setting up a new insurance company, including a foreign investor entering through a joint venture, need to budget for that fee from the outset rather than assume the no-objection stage comes free.

On share transfers generally, the circular sets out Form IRDAI/ToS as the vehicle for seeking prior approval under Regulation 29(5), and relaxes one practical difficulty: where the identity of the transferee is not available or cannot be ascertained at the time of filing, the insurer is not required to furnish those details as a condition of the application. Where the transfer is tied to a proposed listing of the insurer's shares, the applicant must also disclose the purpose and size of the public offer, split between fresh issuance and an offer for sale by existing shareholders, along with the shareholding pattern before and after listing for every shareholder holding more than one per cent of paid-up equity.

Before an insurer approaches a securities regulator to list its shares, Regulation 29(7) now requires it to first intimate IRDAI, accompanied by a signed confirmation from its managing director or chief executive stating that the facts disclosed in the offer documents are true, that every regulatory action IRDAI has taken or initiated against the insurer has been suitably disclosed, and that policyholder interests will be protected through the listing process. The same chapter clarifies that employee stock option exercises above a threshold fixed under Section 6A(4)(b) of the Insurance Act need the regulator's prior approval, a rule the circular says applies to listed insurers as well, requiring them to coordinate compliance with their registrar and transfer agent or depository participant.

For amalgamations, the circular sets out in one place the paperwork an insurer must file with its notice of intention under Regulation 31(1): a draft of the scheme or agreement, the share purchase or subscription agreement, any shareholders' agreement governing the merged entity's management, audited financial statements for the preceding year and the latest quarter for each transacting entity, pro-forma financials of the combined entity, and a report from an independent actuary, one with no professional connection to any party in the five years before signing, assessing the deal's effect on technical reserves, solvency, product pricing and overall financial condition.

Taken together, the changes matter most to the investors and advisers who structure deals in Indian insurance, a sector where foreign participation and periodic consolidation are routine but every step, from an ESOP grant to a full merger, runs through IRDAI's prior approval. A lower transfer fee and a clearer transferee-disclosure rule make routine stake changes marginally cheaper and easier to document, while the new IPO-linked disclosures and the amalgamation checklist give dealmakers a firmer sense of what the regulator will ask for before clearing a transaction, rather than finding out case by case.
why_it_matters: Every change of control, stake sale, listing or merger involving an Indian insurer needs IRDAI's prior clearance, and this circular is the current rulebook for that process. The processing fee for a share-transfer approval drops from Rs 50 lakh to Rs 10 lakh, a real saving for promoters and investors, including foreign strategic partners, structuring a stake change, while new IPO-related disclosures and a consolidated amalgamation document checklist reduce the uncertainty around what IRDAI expects before it will clear a transaction.
card_summary: IRDAI's 2 November 2026 master circular cuts the insurer share-transfer approval fee from Rs 50 lakh to Rs 10 lakh and lays out fresh disclosure rules for IPOs, ESOPs and amalgamations.
card_tip: Share-transfer approvals filed after the 2026 amendment cost Rs 10 lakh in processing fees instead of Rs 50 lakh, but fees paid before that date are not refunded.
verification_notes: The circular number (IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/142/11/2026), its date (2 November 2026), the fee reduction from Rs 50 lakh to Rs 10 lakh under the proviso to Regulation 22(4), the non-refundability of fees paid before the amendment, the new NOC processing fee under Regulation 6(1)(ba), the Form IRDAI/ToS transferee-disclosure relaxation, the IPO-related shareholding disclosure requirements, the pre-listing intimation and MD/CEO confirmation under Regulation 29(7), the ESOP threshold rule under Section 6A(4)(b), and the amalgamation document list under Regulation 31(1) are all read directly from the circular's own text, treated as the primary source. The link to the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act, 2025 and the 30 July 2026 notification date for the amendment regulations are confirmed from Vinod Kothari Consultants' independent commentary. Angel One's figures for the fee cut match the primary text exactly; its description of 'new IPO rules' is reflected in the body only to the extent the primary circular itself confirms. No specific transaction or insurer is named in this circular, so none is attributed to it.
